script.opening: (Breezy, in a hurry, slight wheeze when she laughs.) "Hiya, can I just grab another blue inhaler? I do get through them, I'll admit, but they work — a couple of puffs and I'm grand. I don't really bother with the brown one, I only take that when I remember and I feel fine anyway, so it can't be that bad, can it?"

facts.text: "Most days, if I'm honest. I don't really count" — 2–3 times a day, more when cycling to work or in cold air. Gets through an inhaler roughly every 6–7 weeks.
"Sometimes I wake up coughing. I just use the blue one and go back to sleep. I'm used to it" — 2–3 nights a week.
"I don't think so. Not that I remember" — no A&E or hospital. If asked about steroid tablets: one course from an out-of-hours doctor last winter with a chest infection.

Beclometasone ("the brown one") twice daily on repeat — collected twice this year. "I thought it was for when it's bad. And I forget. It doesn't do anything when I take it, not like the blue." No concerns about steroids when asked.
"Not sure really. I don't pay much attention." If asked specifically: cold air, cats at her friend's, colds. Vapes occasionally at parties; doesn't smoke cigarettes. No ibuprofen problems.
If asked to show: "Like this… shake, puff, breathe in" — fires the puffer then breathes in quickly afterwards; no breath-hold; no spacer.
Asthma since childhood, eczema as a child. Hay fever. No other medicines; combined pill. No allergies. No asthma review for 2 years. Flu jab: no.
Hairdresser, cycles to work. Lives with her boyfriend. Drinks at weekends.

Cheerful and dismissive: "Okay, as long as I get it." If told SABA overuse is a danger sign: "Serious? It works though." Then: "Nobody's really explained it like that." Likes the idea of one inhaler: "So one inhaler instead of two? That's easier. Would I still have a blue one?" If lectured, becomes defensive. If simply given the blue inhaler, leaves happy (the trap).

ice.ideas: "The blue inhaler works, so my asthma can't be that bad. The brown one is for when it's bad."
ice.concerns: She doesn't think there is a problem; she just doesn't want to run out. She has got used to symptoms as normal.
ice.expectations: "Just the blue one so I don't run out."

cues: "I do get through them." — reliever overuse, offered early.
"I'm used to it." — night symptoms normalised.
"It doesn't do anything when I take it." — the preventer misunderstanding.

checkpoints.text: Recognises SABA OVERUSE (7th in 12 months) as a RED-FLAG marker of poorly controlled asthma and increased risk of severe attacks/death — not a benign reissue request

Assesses CONTROL properly — prescription records, a validated questionnaire (Asthma Control Test or Asthma Control Questionnaire), symptom/reliever frequency, night waking, activity limitation, exacerbations/oral-steroid courses, and prior attacks/A&E/admissions/ICU — rather than accepting "I feel fine"

Explains the PREVENTER (ICS treats underlying inflammation, reduces attacks/deaths; reliever only masks) and explores WHY it isn’t taken (beliefs, technique, benefit, access), correcting the "fine on the blue" misconception

Optimises the REGIMEN per NICE NG245 — having addressed adherence and technique, moves her from low-dose ICS plus SABA to low-dose ICS–FORMOTEROL MART — reducing SABA reliance, rather than simply issuing another reliever

Checks inhaler TECHNIQUE, identifies triggers (smoking/allergens/NSAIDs/occupational), provides a PERSONALISED ASTHMA ACTION PLAN, checks flu vaccine eligibility (Green Book chapter 19), and arranges proactive review (spirometry/FeNO/step-up as indicated)

Reframes SABA overuse as a danger signal clearly but without frightening her into disengagement, and reads the "I feel fine" as normalised risk/misconception rather than dismissing the request outright
Explains the preventer/MART rationale in accessible terms, checks understanding (and technique teach-back), and supports adherence

Safety-nets and follows up: red flags of an attack and when to seek emergency help, the action plan, regimen change with review of SABA use and control, and proactive recall — recognising and treating risk, not reissuing a reliever

worked.lbl: Use the request as an opening
worked.txt: "Of course we’ll make sure you’ve got a reliever — but can I be honest? Getting through seven blue inhalers in a year actually tells me your asthma isn’t as well controlled as it feels, and that’s worth a proper look, because it matters for your safety."

"Let me ask: do you wake at night coughing or wheezy? Does it stop you exercising or affect work? Have you needed steroid tablets or A&E in the last year? … Okay. Even though you feel ‘used to it’, those answers tell me there’s room to feel a lot better."

"Here’s the key thing: the blue inhaler only relieves symptoms in the moment — it doesn’t treat the inflammation underneath. The preventer does, and that’s what reduces attacks and keeps you safe. ‘Feeling fine on the blue’ is exactly the trap, because it hides the problem."

"The modern way makes this easier: one inhaler you take regularly that also works as your reliever — so every puff you take when wheezy also delivers the preventer. It cuts down attacks and means you’re not relying on the blue alone. Shall we set that up?"

"Show me how you use it … let’s tweak that. I’ll give you a written action plan so you know what to do if it worsens, and we should look at triggers — smoking, allergies. Are you vaping or smoking at all?"

"If you’re ever using the reliever more and more, breathless at rest, or it’s not lasting, that’s a warning — seek help, and 999 if you can’t speak in sentences. Let’s review you in a few weeks to see how the new inhaler’s working and check your control properly."

f.learning: Frequent reliever (SABA) use is a RED-FLAG marker of poorly controlled asthma and increased risk of severe attacks and asthma DEATH — not a benign request: using 3 or more SABA inhalers a year is associated with more exacerbations and a reliever needed more than twice a week needs review (MHRA Drug Safety Update, April 2025), and the National Review of Asthma Deaths (RCP, 2014) found that many of those who died had been prescribed more than 12 relievers in the previous year, with preventer under-use. So a 7th salbutamol in 12 months with little preventer use demands ASSESSMENT, not a quick reissue. Assess control rather than accept "I feel fine" (NICE NG245: prescription records and a validated questionnaire such as the Asthma Control Test): symptom and reliever frequency, night waking, activity limitation, exacerbations and oral-steroid courses, and prior attacks/A&E/admissions/ICU (the strongest predictors of future risk) — frequent SABA use IS uncontrolled asthma even when normalised. Explain that the inhaled CORTICOSTEROID preventer treats the underlying airway inflammation and reduces attacks and deaths whereas the reliever only masks symptoms, and explore why the preventer is not taken (steroid beliefs, "only when bad", no perceived benefit, poor technique, access) — correcting the dangerous "fine on the blue" misconception. Optimise the regimen per NICE NG245: after addressing adherence, technique and triggers, move someone not controlled on low-dose ICS plus SABA to low-dose ICS–FORMOTEROL MART (a single inhaler used daily and as reliever, so every reliever puff delivers anti-inflammatory ICS; as-needed ICS/formoterol alone is the starting point for new diagnoses), reducing SABA reliance and exacerbations — the marks are in recognising risk and optimising, not adding another blue inhaler. Check inhaler technique, identify triggers (smoking/allergens/NSAIDs/occupational), provide a personalised asthma action plan, check flu vaccine eligibility (Green Book chapter 19), and arrange proactive review (moderate-dose MART, then objective tests and specialist advice, if still uncontrolled). Reframe SABA overuse clearly but without frightening the patient into disengagement, and safety-net for attacks.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG245 (asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management, 2024, joint with BTS and SIGN) · [2] MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2025): SABA overuse in asthma · [3] RCP National Review of Asthma Deaths, Why asthma still kills (2014) · [4] NICE QS25 (asthma, 2013, updated 2018) · [5] UKHSA Green Book chapter 19 (influenza) · [6] NICE NG209 (tobacco, 2021) · [7] BNF
knowledge.summary: Seven relievers in a year with little preventer is uncontrolled, high-risk asthma, not a repeat request. Assess control, find out why the preventer is not used, check technique, then move her to low-dose MART with ICS/formoterol so every reliever dose also treats inflammation. Never issue a SABA without an ICS.

points.t: MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2025) [2]: overuse of SABA, with or without maintenance therapy, is linked to severe attacks and death; do not prescribe a SABA without a concomitant ICS, and review anyone needing their reliever more than twice a week. Using 3 or more SABA inhalers a year is associated with more exacerbations. The National Review of Asthma Deaths [3] found excess reliever and too little preventer prescribing in many of those who died.

NICE NG245 [1]: uncontrolled asthma includes any exacerbation needing oral corticosteroids, or frequent symptoms such as using a reliever on 3 or more days a week or night waking 1 or more times a week. Check prescription records for reliever and preventer issues, oral steroid courses and emergency attendances; consider a validated questionnaire such as the Asthma Control Test or Asthma Control Questionnaire.

NICE NG245 [1]: before starting or changing medicines, address possible reasons for poor control — adherence, inhaler technique, alternative diagnoses and triggers such as smoking. Check adherence and technique at every review.

NICE NG245 [1]: for people aged 12 and over whose asthma is not controlled on regular low-dose ICS plus as-needed SABA, consider low-dose MART — one ICS/formoterol inhaler taken regularly and as the reliever, usually with no separate SABA. For newly diagnosed asthma, as-needed ICS/formoterol (AIR) is the starting point. Device, dose and maximum daily puffs per BNF [7].

Give a personalised written asthma action plan: usual treatment, signs of worsening, what to do, and when to get emergency help. NICE QS25 [4] includes a personalised action plan and monitoring of control at each review.
Ask about smoking and vaping (NICE NG209 [6]: very brief advice and referral), allergens, NSAIDs and work exposures. Check flu vaccine eligibility under Green Book chapter 19 [5].

Review within a few weeks of the switch: control, technique, how often she needs extra doses, and any oral steroid use. If still uncontrolled on low-dose MART, NG245 [1] steps up to moderate-dose MART and then objective tests and specialist advice.

dg.d: Open start; acknowledged the reliever request and promised she would not go without, before exploring.
Impact on sleep, work and activity; forgetting and routine; smoking or vaping asked.
Prescription record review, validated control questionnaire, technique check on video; objective tests if control stays poor.
Uncontrolled asthma from preventer non-use versus poor technique, triggers or an alternative diagnosis.
Asked about oral steroid courses, A&E attendances, admissions, night waking and reliever frequency.
Named uncontrolled, high-risk asthma from SABA overuse and ICS under-use.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Low-dose MART (NICE NG245); no SABA without ICS; technique corrected; written action plan.
Triggers and smoking addressed; flu vaccine eligibility; adherence support she chose.
Same-day and 999 red flags; teach-back; review in about four weeks.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I’m used to it” and “it doesn’t do anything” and explored both.
Idea (the blue inhaler works so asthma can’t be bad), concern (running out), expectation (quick reissue).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — She doesn't think there is a problem; she just doesn't want to run out. She has got used to symptoms as normal — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Tanya, I’m Dr Rahman. Thanks for joining. I know you asked for another blue inhaler — tell me how your asthma has been.
model.why: Open start that acknowledges her request

model.text: Fine, honestly. I get through the blue ones, but a couple of puffs and I’m grand. I don’t bother much with the brown one. I feel fine, so it can’t be that bad, can it?
I’ll make sure you’re not left without a reliever today — I promise that. Can I spend a few minutes on how your asthma is really doing? It’s worth it, and then we’ll sort the inhaler.
model.why: Reassures on the request and agrees an agenda

model.text: Okay, as long as I get it.
How many days a week do you find yourself using the blue one?
Most days, if I’m honest. I don’t really count.
Does your asthma ever wake you at night, or stop you doing things — exercise, work, getting about?
Sometimes I wake up coughing. I just use the blue one and go back to sleep. I’m used to it.
Have you needed steroid tablets, out-of-hours help or A&E for your chest in the last year, or ever been in hospital with it?
model.why: Exacerbations and past severe attacks — the strongest risk markers

model.text: I don’t think so. Not that I remember.
I’ll check the record too. Tell me about the brown one — what do you understand it does, and what gets in the way of taking it?
model.why: Explores beliefs and barriers to the preventer

model.text: I thought it was for when it’s bad. And I forget. It doesn’t do anything when I take it, not like the blue.
That’s really helpful, and a lot of people think exactly that. Anything you’ve noticed sets it off? And do you smoke or vape at all?
Not sure really. I don’t pay much attention.
When you think about your asthma, is anything worrying you about it — or about the inhalers?
Not really. I just want the blue one so I don’t run out.

Can I be honest with you? Seven blue inhalers in a year, using it most days and waking at night, tells me your asthma isn’t as settled as it feels. The blue inhaler opens the airways for a few hours, but it doesn’t treat the swelling inside them that causes attacks. Relying on it is one of the things that puts people at risk of a serious attack.
model.why: Reframes SABA overuse as a risk marker with a reason

model.text: Serious? It works though.

It does, in the moment — that’s the catch. It hides the problem. The brown one works quietly on the swelling, which is why you don’t feel it doing anything. I’m not saying this to scare you; I’m saying it because it’s very fixable.
model.why: Corrects the misconception without frightening her

model.text: Nobody’s really explained it like that.

Here’s an idea that fits how you use inhalers. There’s a single combination inhaler with a preventer and a quick-acting reliever in it. You take it every day, and when you’re wheezy you take an extra puff of the same inhaler instead of the blue one. So every time you reach for relief, you’re also treating the swelling.
model.why: Offers low-dose MART as NG245 recommends for uncontrolled ICS plus SABA

model.text: So one inhaler instead of two? That’s easier. Would I still have a blue one?

Usually you wouldn’t need it — the new one is your reliever. I’ll explain how many extra puffs you can take in a day and what to do if you’re using more than that. Could you show me how you take your inhaler now? Hold it up so I can see.
model.why: Explains the plan and checks technique on video

model.text: Like this… shake, puff, breathe in.

Nearly — try breathing out fully first, then a slow, steady breath in as you press, and hold it for about ten seconds. The pharmacist can check it with the new device too. I’ll also send you a written asthma action plan so you know what to do if it gets worse.
model.why: Corrects technique and provides an action plan

model.text: Okay. That’s fine.
What do you think you’ll find hardest about the new way?
model.why: Checks feasibility and invites her view

model.text: Remembering the morning dose, probably.
A lot of people keep it by their toothbrush or set a phone reminder. Would either work for you?
model.why: Supports adherence with her own choice

model.text: Toothbrush. I can do that.

If you need extra puffs more and more, if it’s not lasting, or you’re breathless even at rest, contact us the same day. If you can’t speak in full sentences, your lips look blue, or it isn’t helping at all, call 999.
model.why: Specific attack red flags and when to act

model.text: Okay.
So I know I’ve explained it well — tell me how you’ll use the new inhaler.
Every morning and night, plus a puff when I’m wheezy instead of the blue one. And ring you if I’m using it loads.
Exactly right. I’ll review you in about four weeks to see how you’re getting on, and check whether you’re due a flu jab. Thanks, Tanya.

social.t: Young adults often accept night cough and breathlessness as normal. Routine, forgetting and the lack of felt benefit from ICS are common barriers.
In England, a prescription prepayment certificate can reduce costs for people paying for several items; one combination inhaler may also reduce the number of items.

legal.t: MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2025): do not prescribe a SABA without a concomitant ICS. Practices should have a system that flags excess reliever requests for clinical review.

professional.t: A seventh reliever request should trigger a review, not an automatic reissue (GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices, 2021: review repeat prescriptions).
Explain options and respect her choice of regimen and adherence prompt; document the discussion and the plan.

community.t: Community pharmacy New Medicine Service when a new inhaler starts, inhaler technique videos from Asthma + Lung UK, and practice asthma nurse review.

redFlags: Previous severe or near-fatal attack, ICU or admission
Oral steroid courses or A&E attendances in the last year
Reliever needed most days, night waking, or relief lasting less time
Breathless at rest or unable to speak in sentences — emergency
psychosocial: What she believes the preventer does
Routine, forgetting, and lack of felt benefit
Smoking or vaping, work and home triggers
ice: Idea: “The blue works, so it can’t be that bad.”
Concern: running out of her reliever
Expectation: a quick blue inhaler reissue

playbook.diagnosis: “Needing the blue inhaler most days and seven in a year means your asthma isn’t controlled, even though you feel used to it. It’s the swelling in the airways that isn’t being treated.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The blue inhaler is like opening a window when a room is smoky. The preventer puts out the fire. You’ve been opening windows for a year.”

management.reflectIce: “You said the blue one works — and it does, for a few hours. That’s exactly why it can hide what’s going on underneath.”
management.psychosocial: Use her preference for a single inhaler; link the dose to a habit she already has; avoid scare tactics.
sharedPlan: Low-dose MART with an ICS/formoterol inhaler (NICE NG245); no separate SABA usually needed; dose and daily maximum per BNF
Technique check and correction; pharmacy New Medicine Service
Written personalised asthma action plan; triggers and smoking; flu vaccine eligibility
safetyNet: Same day: needing more and more extra puffs, relief not lasting, breathless at rest
999: can’t speak in sentences, blue lips, no response to reliever

pitfalls.intro: This station hides a high-risk patient inside a routine request. The marks are in recognising the risk, understanding why the preventer isn’t used, and changing the regimen — not in reciting asthma death statistics.

items.fail: Reissuing salbutamol and suggesting she books an asthma review “sometime”.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” MHRA (April 2025) and NICE NG245 treat SABA reliance as a safety issue.
items.fix: Review now: control, risk, preventer use, and a regimen change today.

items.fail: Doubling the ICS or adding a LABA without checking adherence or technique.
items.why: NICE NG245 says address adherence, technique and triggers before changing medicines.
items.fix: Ask what gets in the way, check technique on video, then change the regimen.

items.fail: Leaving her on ICS plus SABA with a stern word about adherence.
items.why: For uncontrolled asthma on regular low-dose ICS plus SABA, NG245 recommends considering low-dose MART.
items.fix: Offer the single ICS/formoterol inhaler for daily and reliever use.

items.fail: Opening with “You could die from overusing this.”
items.why: “Uses fear rather than explanation.” She switches off and may not return.
items.fix: Explain why the blue hides the problem, then show the fix.

items.fail: Not asking what she thinks the brown inhaler does.
items.why: Her belief (“only when it’s bad”, “it doesn’t do anything”) is the root of the problem; missing it misses the cue.
items.fix: “What do you understand it does, and what gets in the way?”

items.fail: No action plan, no technique check, no follow-up date.
items.why: Vague closure is a common failing statement in long-term condition stations.
items.fix: Written action plan, technique on screen, teach-back, review in four weeks.

timeMap.d: Promise she won’t be left without a reliever, then ask for a few minutes on control.
Reliever days per week, night waking, activity, oral steroids, A&E, admissions, preventer beliefs, triggers, smoking.
“It works so it can’t be bad”; wants to avoid running out.
Seven relievers a year is a warning sign; blue relieves, preventer treats.
Low-dose MART, technique, action plan, adherence tip, red flags, teach-back, review in four weeks.

wordPics.fail: Reissues salbutamol without comment; or refuses it and lectures about asthma deaths; never asks about night symptoms or oral steroids; no action plan.
wordPics.pass: Recognises SABA overuse as poor control, assesses control, explains preventer versus reliever, changes the regimen and gives an action plan with review.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explores why the preventer isn’t used and answers it; offers low-dose MART as NG245 recommends; corrects technique on screen; agrees an adherence prompt she chose; teach-back; she leaves engaged rather than frightened.

avoid.dont: “Seven inhalers? People die from overusing these.”
avoid.instead: “Seven in a year tells me your asthma isn’t as settled as it feels — and it’s very fixable.”
avoid.why: Fear without a plan drives disengagement.

avoid.dont: “I can’t give you another blue inhaler.”
avoid.instead: “You won’t be left without a reliever. Let’s make sure it’s the right one.”
avoid.why: Refusing a reliever is unsafe; changing to a combination reliever is the fix.

avoid.dont: “You need to take your brown inhaler twice a day.” (and nothing more)
avoid.instead: “What gets in the way of taking the brown one?”
avoid.why: Instructions without understanding her beliefs rarely change behaviour.

SCA_MODELS.text: Toothbrush. I can do that.

If you need extra puffs more and more, if it’s not lasting, or you’re breathless even at rest, contact us the same day. If you can’t speak in full sentences, your lips look blue, or it isn’t helping at all, call 999.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific attack red flags and when to act

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay.
So I know I’ve explained it well — tell me how you’ll use the new inhaler.
Every morning and night, plus a puff when I’m wheezy instead of the blue one. And ring you if I’m using it loads.
Exactly right. I’ll review you in about four weeks to see how you’re getting on, and check whether you’re due a flu jab. Thanks, Tanya.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG245 (asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management, 2024, joint with BTS and SIGN) · [2] MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2025): SABA overuse in asthma · [3] RCP National Review of Asthma Deaths, Why asthma still kills (2014) · [4] NICE QS25 (asthma, 2013, updated 2018) · [5] UKHSA Green Book chapter 19 (influenza) · [6] NICE NG209 (tobacco, 2021) · [7] BNF
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Seven relievers in a year with little preventer is uncontrolled, high-risk asthma, not a repeat request. Assess control, find out why the preventer is not used, check technique, then move her to low-dose MART with ICS/formoterol so every reliever dose also treats inflammation. Never issue a SABA without an ICS.

points.t: MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2025) [2]: overuse of SABA, with or without maintenance therapy, is linked to severe attacks and death; do not prescribe a SABA without a concomitant ICS, and review anyone needing their reliever more than twice a week. Using 3 or more SABA inhalers a year is associated with more exacerbations. The National Review of Asthma Deaths [3] found excess reliever and too little preventer prescribing in many of those who died.

NICE NG245 [1]: uncontrolled asthma includes any exacerbation needing oral corticosteroids, or frequent symptoms such as using a reliever on 3 or more days a week or night waking 1 or more times a week. Check prescription records for reliever and preventer issues, oral steroid courses and emergency attendances; consider a validated questionnaire such as the Asthma Control Test or Asthma Control Questionnaire.

NICE NG245 [1]: before starting or changing medicines, address possible reasons for poor control — adherence, inhaler technique, alternative diagnoses and triggers such as smoking. Check adherence and technique at every review.

NICE NG245 [1]: for people aged 12 and over whose asthma is not controlled on regular low-dose ICS plus as-needed SABA, consider low-dose MART — one ICS/formoterol inhaler taken regularly and as the reliever, usually with no separate SABA. For newly diagnosed asthma, as-needed ICS/formoterol (AIR) is the starting point. Device, dose and maximum daily puffs per BNF [7].

Give a personalised written asthma action plan: usual treatment, signs of worsening, what to do, and when to get emergency help. NICE QS25 [4] includes a personalised action plan and monitoring of control at each review.
Ask about smoking and vaping (NICE NG209 [6]: very brief advice and referral), allergens, NSAIDs and work exposures. Check flu vaccine eligibility under Green Book chapter 19 [5].

Review within a few weeks of the switch: control, technique, how often she needs extra doses, and any oral steroid use. If still uncontrolled on low-dose MART, NG245 [1] steps up to moderate-dose MART and then objective tests and specialist advice.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; acknowledged the reliever request and promised she would not go without, before exploring.
Impact on sleep, work and activity; forgetting and routine; smoking or vaping asked.
Picked up “I’m used to it” and “it doesn’t do anything” and explored both.
Idea (the blue inhaler works so asthma can’t be bad), concern (running out), expectation (quick reissue).
Prescription record review, validated control questionnaire, technique check on video; objective tests if control stays poor.
Uncontrolled asthma from preventer non-use versus poor technique, triggers or an alternative diagnosis.
Asked about oral steroid courses, A&E attendances, admissions, night waking and reliever frequency.
Named uncontrolled, high-risk asthma from SABA overuse and ICS under-use.
Low-dose MART (NICE NG245); no SABA without ICS; technique corrected; written action plan.
Triggers and smoking addressed; flu vaccine eligibility; adherence support she chose.
Same-day and 999 red flags; teach-back; review in about four weeks.

social.t: Young adults often accept night cough and breathlessness as normal. Routine, forgetting and the lack of felt benefit from ICS are common barriers.
In England, a prescription prepayment certificate can reduce costs for people paying for several items; one combination inhaler may also reduce the number of items.

legal.t: MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2025): do not prescribe a SABA without a concomitant ICS. Practices should have a system that flags excess reliever requests for clinical review.

professional.t: A seventh reliever request should trigger a review, not an automatic reissue (GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices, 2021: review repeat prescriptions).
Explain options and respect her choice of regimen and adherence prompt; document the discussion and the plan.

community.t: Community pharmacy New Medicine Service when a new inhaler starts, inhaler technique videos from Asthma + Lung UK, and practice asthma nurse review.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Needing the blue inhaler most days and seven in a year means your asthma isn’t controlled, even though you feel used to it. It’s the swelling in the airways that isn’t being treated.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The blue inhaler is like opening a window when a room is smoky. The preventer puts out the fire. You’ve been opening windows for a year.”

management.reflectIce: “You said the blue one works — and it does, for a few hours. That’s exactly why it can hide what’s going on underneath.”
management.psychosocial: Use her preference for a single inhaler; link the dose to a habit she already has; avoid scare tactics.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station hides a high-risk patient inside a routine request. The marks are in recognising the risk, understanding why the preventer isn’t used, and changing the regimen — not in reciting asthma death statistics.

items.fail: Reissuing salbutamol and suggesting she books an asthma review “sometime”.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” MHRA (April 2025) and NICE NG245 treat SABA reliance as a safety issue.
items.fix: Review now: control, risk, preventer use, and a regimen change today.

items.fail: Doubling the ICS or adding a LABA without checking adherence or technique.
items.why: NICE NG245 says address adherence, technique and triggers before changing medicines.
items.fix: Ask what gets in the way, check technique on video, then change the regimen.

items.fail: Leaving her on ICS plus SABA with a stern word about adherence.
items.why: For uncontrolled asthma on regular low-dose ICS plus SABA, NG245 recommends considering low-dose MART.
items.fix: Offer the single ICS/formoterol inhaler for daily and reliever use.

items.fail: Opening with “You could die from overusing this.”
items.why: “Uses fear rather than explanation.” She switches off and may not return.
items.fix: Explain why the blue hides the problem, then show the fix.

items.fail: Not asking what she thinks the brown inhaler does.
items.why: Her belief (“only when it’s bad”, “it doesn’t do anything”) is the root of the problem; missing it misses the cue.
items.fix: “What do you understand it does, and what gets in the way?”

items.fail: No action plan, no technique check, no follow-up date.
items.why: Vague closure is a common failing statement in long-term condition stations.
items.fix: Written action plan, technique on screen, teach-back, review in four weeks.
